utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, doctor. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence which still applies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Doctor, on Friday, you told us that you were taken to Sremska Mitrovica. Do you remember that, giving that evidence?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I haven't very many questions for you but let's just deal with one or two aspects. I think it's also correct to say, is it not, that you were taken to a -- what is called a higher military court; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was taken before an institution called the higher military court in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if I deal with it in general terms, you were charged with organising an armed rebellion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Also accused of carrying out organ transplant and selling human organs to Germany and France; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I did ask you about two doctors last Friday; one was called Ivankovic. Did Ivankovic come to give evidence against you at that court hearing?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that court hearing, which was never completed, Dr. Ivankovic did not turn up, nor did the other doctor we spoke about last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And did you ask the Serbian authorities or the authorities in charge of that court hearing to produce those witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that court, I asked that witnesses be brought in, and that we face each other, and that then they tell me how it was possible to sell organs when there have to be specially trained teams to do that. I believe that in most clinics throughout Europe not every surgical team knows how to take organs from corpses or those who have just died.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: And if we deal with it this way, is it correct that nothing was ever proved against you and you were eventually, I believe, exchanged?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. It's impossible to prove something that never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I have no further questions for you. Thank you very much, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I believe that at this point in time it would be wise for Mr. Domazet to cross-examine the witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would be delighted, yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Good day to everybody and good day to the witness, Dr. Njavro. Let me introduce myself. My name is Vladomir Domazet. I am co-counsel for Mr. Mrksic. Doctor, I would just like to go through some information from your curriculum. You've already said something about this. And as I gather from your responses to my learned friend you were not born in Vukovar. You came to Vukovar after completing your medical studies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And your education took place in your native area, which is quite a different part of the country. You were educated up to your military service in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. I completed primary school in Herzegovina, in my native village, high school for the most part in Dubrovnik. After that, I passed the exam after eight -- after secondary school and then I went to the faculty of medicine in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You served your military service in Capljina where you were registered. That's why I thought you had been living there.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the then regulations of the military authorities, you had to report for military service from your place of birth and from your place of origin. I was completing my studies at the faculty of medicine, and therefore I could not be officially registered as working and living somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me where and when you did your military service in the then JNA?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did my military service in the then JNA in Novi Sad. First, in the Miletic Barracks, in 1966 and 1967. After that, in the outpatients' clinic at the garrison at Petrovaradin.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was your military service in the medical corps or in an armed unit?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first two or three months, I went through the standard military training, after which I was in the medical corps, as I said, in the outpatients' clinic, in the barracks, in the garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: After completing your military service, and after graduating from the faculty of medicine in Zagreb, your first job, as I understand it, was in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: With respect to this job, I would like to dwell for a moment on the period after your specialist residence, when you were already a surgeon, a specialist in surgery. Can you tell me, in the relevant time period, that is in 1991, how many surgeons were there in total in the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the Vukovar Hospital -- just a moment, please. Four. In 1991 and throughout the aggression against Croatia and the town of Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Four surgeons, including yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me their names of the other three, that is?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Mladen Ivankovic, Dr. Mirko Stanojevic, and Dr. Lazo Manojlovic, and Dr. Juraj Njavro.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Njavro, in Friday -- on Friday, I think, when answering my learned friend's questions, I think you mentioned that you were the only surgeon who was of Croat ethnicity. Is this correct? Were the other three of other ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The only one among those four who was a Croat was myself. The other three were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And your chief or the chief of the surgical ward at the time was Dr. Ivankovic, as far as I can understand?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Dr. Ivankovic was the chief of surgery throughout, but I was the chief of the wartime medical service for the Vukovar Hospital and the Vukovar municipality, according to the decision of the main medical staff in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Will you tell me when this decision was issued and from when you were in charge of the war hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometime from, I think, the end of July or towards the end of July 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did I understand you correctly, that you were appointed head or chief of the war hospital? Does that mean that Dr. Ivankovic stopped being the chief of the surgical ward?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No one deprived him of that part of his responsibility. He was still in charge of the surgical ward.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now that we are discussing this topic, doctor, can you tell me what your role specifically was in this war hospital that was different from your previous regular duties and obligations?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: What has to be done in wartime, that's to say, providing for sufficient quantities of sanitary materiel and medicine so that the town, which had 45.000 inhabitants before the war, would not be threatened as regards medical care for lack of medicines and other material. During the fierce aggression in August, the supplies proved to be insufficient which ultimately led to large numbers of wounded and also patients who were simply ill could not be provided with adequate medical assistance, not because the medical team was not sufficiently well-trained, but because it was impossible to bring in medicines and sanitary and medical material and equipment necessary for proper and professional treatment. This was due to the blockade of Vukovar, the siege, and that is why, at least we doctors think that some wounded or sick patients came to a tragic end, for the simple reason that, as I said, it was impossible to bring in medical supplies and medicines. Also blood infusions, blood substitutes, infusions, equipment needed for reanimation. I can give you some tragic examples where, in spite of the greatest care, due to lack of medicines and because the hospital was so badly damaged and also because of the numbers of wounded whom it was impossible to evacuate, there were people who ended up tragically, in spite of the treatment. The shelling and destruction contributed to this. It came from all sides, from the air, from the water, from the ground, and you could only live underground. Underground it's easier for infections to spread because, as I said, due to the shelling, it was impossible to bring in water, food, medicines, and what little we had in the hospital had to be distributed very rationally. At one point, precisely because it was impossible to maintain the required hygiene, diseases turned up which are sometimes characteristic of war, where it was impossible to help people because, I repeat, because of the blockade and the daily destruction of the hospital, we couldn't get the necessary serums to prevent certain diseases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, I apologise, I have to interrupt you. I have a request for you. We will get to the topics that you have mentioned just now later on. During examination-in-chief you had opportunity to touch upon some of those topics. I would now like to ask you to answer in specific terms to my questions, and you will be given an opportunity to expand on your answers later on. My question pertained to your role as chief of the war hospital, which existed at the time. You said you were appointed to that post in late July and then you went on to discuss some other matters. I would now like to ask you to explain something else to us. In addition to ensuring that there were sufficient supplies of medication and so on, were any other preparations conducted in terms of personnel, organisation and so on?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No other preparations were made except that we received aid in the form of several ambulances. In addition to that, the main medical staff in Zagreb sent several times a team of doctors and nurses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. We will return to the issue of the hospital surgery and these other topics that you have touched upon. But prior to that, I would like to turn to something else. I believe that you are well-informed or will be able to tell me about something that took place prior to 1991. This has to do with the first multi-party elections which were held in all republics of the former Yugoslavia, including Croatia. They were held in 1990; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In Croatia, at the level of the Republic of Croatia, it was the Croatian Democratic Union that won; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you agree or perhaps do you hold another opinion about the Croatian Democratic Union being the political party with a nationalistic orientation?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a politician. I can't discuss politics, and I cannot evaluate political platforms of various political parties. At the time, I was not a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember those elections? Do you remember whether in the elections the Serbs in Croatia had their own national party?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly -- but once again I have to qualify this by saying that I was not politically active in any way, because up until nineteen-ninety something I never belonged to any party. Therefore, I couldn't tell you exactly how many political parties participated, who was on the ballots, and so on. And I think that I can say with certainty that I was not sufficiently active in that regard, nor did I participate in any preparations. My role was that of an ordinary, loyal citizen who went to vote in elections. And I voted in accordance with my conscience.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, if I understood you well, you cannot remember, or perhaps you never knew, whether, in those first multi-party elections in Croatia, the Serbs had their own national party?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they did, that the Serbs did have their national party, because if, as you said, the Croats had their national party, which was the HDZ, then it follows that the Serbs also had their own political party. When one passed through Vukovar, I was able to see various advertisements and so on, and all of them appealed to their voters, including the Serbian party, which was called the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that in those days in 1990, when the first multi-party elections were held, you believe that the SDS took part in the elections?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that's right. We have already said that there were a number of political parties in the elections, from which it follows that the SDS also took part, alongside other legally recognised political parties which were eligible to take part in the elections. SDS had to be among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the time, you'd been living in Vukovar for quite a long time, and as you told us, you voted in the elections in Vukovar. Do you remember which party won the local elections in Vukovar then?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember. Perhaps I knew it at the time, but as I've already told you, back in 1990, that wasn't something that I paid a lot of attention to, nor tried to remember those facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I were to remind you and tell you that it was the party of democratic changes led by Mr. Ivica Racan, its chairman, would you agree with me or you don't remember?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to confirm what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember who was elected president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar in those local elections that I asked you about?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that there were a lot of negotiations on that issue, yes. It was very important who would be elected president of municipality, and I believe that it was Mr. Slavko Dokmanovic who was elected president of the Vukovar municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's right. Mr. Dokmanovic was elected. Do you remember perhaps now or do you know to what party he belonged and what party he represented in the elections?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I've told you, I think that that was a very contentious issue and that it took consensus to reach an agreement. I don't remember what political party he belonged to. I know he was a Serb, but as for the political party, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember perhaps, Mr. Njavro, who was vice-president of the municipal assembly of Vukovar after those elections?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is the name Marin Vidic, known as Bili, familiar to you?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Marin Vidic, Bili, later on was the government commissioner. But I don't remember him being vice-president of the Vukovar municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Even though you told me that at the time you were not active in politics and were not interested in politics by your own account, do you remember that after those elections in late 1990 the constitution of the Republic of Croatia was amended?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know that there was a lot of debate about those amendments and that finally what the amendments set forth was that the Serbs as a nation were no longer a constituent nation of the Republic of Croatia but that, rather, that status was awarded solely to Croats?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that in the assembly of Croatia, it was adopted that the sovereign nation in the Republic of Croatia was the Croat nation and that everybody else constituted national minorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember perhaps, Mr. Njavro, or do you know how many Serbs resided in Croatia as citizens of Croatia and also in Vukovar at around that time when those amendments were passed?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the figures for Croatia but I know them for Vukovar. In Vukovar, or rather in the municipality of Vukovar, there were 44 per cent of Croats residing there, 37 per cent of Serbs, or perhaps 38 per cent of Serbs, 37 at least and perhaps a percentage or two more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, after that constitution was adopted, do you remember that certain tensions arose and that inter-ethnic relations in Croatia as a whole deteriorated and in Vukovar as well?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I couldn't claim that as regards Vukovar. As for Croatia, to tell you the truth, at the time, I lived in Vukovar, I was preoccupied with Vukovar problems, so I know only what pertains to Vukovar. As for the broader picture, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, you believed that this did not cause any deterioration in inter-ethnic relations in Vukovar or any tensions?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no particular or remarkable tensions. I don't remember there being any at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When I asked you about Mr. Marin Vidic, you said that you didn't remember him being vice-president of the municipal assembly, but that you did remember him being appointed government commissioner. Do you remember how it came about that, instead of legitimate and legally elected authorities, a government commissioner was appointed to administer the municipality?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've told you, I am not aware of those events. I was not interested in politics. I devoted myself to medicine, medical problems, and I didn't know these things. If what you say is true, if Marin Vidic was indeed removed from the position of vice-president of the municipal assembly and appointed government commissioner, I would have no reason to know those things, because, as I've told you, at the time, politics was not my occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You told us, and it is true, that Mr. Marin Vidovic was appointed person in charge of the municipality. This is something that you told us. Now I'm asking you whether you know how this came about and when.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I lived in Vukovar. Therefore, I had to know who was the person in charge, and whom one had to go and see about certain problems. Therefore, I knew that Marin Vidic, Bili, was appointed government commissioner, but how this came about, I really don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know what political party he belonged to?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You didn't know it at the time nor later?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know to this day what political party he belongs to, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: As you have said to us that you were not involved in politics at the time, were not a member of any political party, I will still try to press on and ask you whether you remember that in your contacts - and you must have had a lot because you were a doctor and you met a lot of people every day - you learned what were the activities of certain political parties, and here I have in mind mostly the HDZ, in respect of fund raising and creating various units and groups and so on in villages and in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about that. I was a doctor, and my main focus was to deal with the patients, people who came to me with various problems. I had to diagnose them, so I dealt with that. I did not engage in finding out what kind of rumours circulated the town. God knows whether those stories were true or just hearsay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If these were just stories or hearsay that you paid no attention to, did you perhaps register that roadblocks were coming up around various roads and villages and that obstacles were created to normal travel and free movement? Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I knew about this because I had personal experience; namely, on the 2nd of May 1991, in the morning, early, I set out to go to Osijek. I was to take a patient to be examined there, to have a head scan, CAT-scan. On my way back, my wife and I were stopped at the roadblock in Trpinja. At that roadblock, I saw for the first time paramilitary men dressed in Chetnik uniforms, who let us through the village, and we were the only ones to be allowed to pass because I had operated on one of the relatives of the -- of one of the men manning the roadblock. He told us to go to the other part of the village to report to another roadblock where we were to report to somebody who would then ensure our passage onwards. Ilija Mirkic, a resident of Trpinja, ensured that we could pass through. He was the man, manning the roadblock at this other point in the village where we were also met with armed individuals wearing cockades and typical Chetnik insignia. This is how I managed to reach the hospital in Vukovar. The wounded policemen from Borovo Selo had already been brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Trpinja, the village you mentioned, does that mean, based on what you just told us, that that was a village predominantly populated by Serbs or exclusively populated by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could say that it was exclusively populated by Serbs. I don't know whether there were any Croats, if any. In the village I saw armed people in front of the houses. In one of the houses I even saw a group of people. Those were armed paramilitary members dressed in Chetnik uniforms. They were gathered in a room in a house in the middle of a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, when you say Chetniks and you used -- you have used that term quite frequently throughout your testimony, perhaps it would be a good idea to explain to the Trial Chamber and everybody else who Chetniks were and how were you yourself able to recognise them as Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was able to recognise them because Seselj, when frequently touring Baranja and Borovo Selo, was shown on television wearing Chetnik uniforms, Chetnik insignia, and advocating Chetnik policy which was aimed against all non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. You said that you saw men in Trpinja who looked like Chetniks. How were you able to identify them as Chetniks?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chetniks have their insignia and threats. One of the Chetniks approached us with a sniper rifle and said, "I am a Chetnik." My wife, who drove the car and who didn't halt immediately upon hearing his order was told by him, "I as a Chetnik could have killed you. This time I saved your life. Do not return here and do not pass through Trpinja again." If he said this, I had no reason to doubt that he was not a Chetnik and that others dressed alike and wearing the same insignia were not Chetniks either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know or did you hear at the time why was the roadblock set up in Trpinja and what led to this village being isolated? How did this come about, if there indeed were no tensions prior to that, no deterioration in interethnic relations, as you've told us?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw no reasons for this either, and this is why I was so surprised. That morning I went to Osijek, which is 35 kilometres away. Trpinja is the first village when one travels from Vukovar to Osijek, and following it are Klisa and another village. In the morning I passed, there were no obstacles and on my way back, at around 11.00 or so, I came to Trpinja -- or rather, I came to Klisa, which is also a predominantly Serb village, and there was nothing there. And it wasn't until I reached Trpinja that I saw roadblocks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know that similar roadblocks were erected in villages populated predominantly by Croats?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that because neither then nor later did I go and visit any Croat or Serb villages. Therefore, I couldn't know for a fact whether roadblocks were erected in Croat villages as well, not just in Serb villages. I spent almost 24 hours a day in the hospital on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You said it was -- precisely on that day that there was a fierce clash in Borovo Selo where more than one policeman was killed and that on your return to the hospital you were involved in this as a surgeon. Does this event, that is, the roadblocks in Trpinja which were not there on your way to Osijek but only on the way back, does it strike you as a response to the event in Borovo Selo? Do you think that these people were afraid that a large number of policemen might come to their village as they had come to Borovo Selo and there might be another clash?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't believe that was the reason, because to get to Borovo Selo you have to pass through Borovo, which is part of Vukovar, whereas Trpinja, Klisa, Bobota, Vera, the whole area to the north of Vukovar municipality, were villages with a majority or perhaps entirely Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know what the distance is, approximately, between Trpinja and Borovo Selo?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me a minute to consider. Maybe five, six or more kilometres, but I don't think it's more than ten, or thereabouts. Maybe a little less. I never really paid attention to that, but as I see it, because I know both places, that's the approximate distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In any case, these places are very close to each other and it's very easy to reach one from the other. However, the chief event of the day was what happened in Borovo Selo, and you mentioned this while being examined by Mr. Moore as well as now. So at the same time as the events you describe in Trpinja, there was a fierce armed clash in Borovo Selo in which there were killed and wounded on both sides; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were people killed on the Croatian side. I'm referring to policemen. And 12 were brought to the area in front of the hospital and the MUP building, or, rather, that's the police station in Vukovar. And there was a group of wounded, if I recall rightly, because that was the beginning. That's why it's easier to remember the numbers. I think there were some 20-odd wounded, and this included both policemen and members of paramilitary units from Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, if I understood you correctly, you are saying that those 12 policemen who had been killed were even brought to the Vukovar Hospital, that the corpses of the policemen were brought there at the same time as the wounded?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point in time, I was not in the hospital. I was on my way back through the roadblock in Trpinja, as I described. When I arrived at the hospital, the dead had already been brought there. I was told that some of them had been brought to the hospital but then they were taken away to the cemetery at Mitnica. Some of the other dead were in front of the police station and from there, in order for a post mortem to be carried out, they were taken to the new cemetery at Mitnica. The wounded were in the hospital and were being examined. Therefore, I joined in the work on examining them. We hospitalised them. I think there were 21 or 22 wounded from Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand correctly, all the dead were brought to Vukovar on that day. When you speak of the wounded, I think you said that some of the wounded were from the side of the Croatian police and the rest were citizens of Borovo Selo. Did I understand you correctly to say that these wounded too were brought to your hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Some of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Some of all the wounded or ...

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were wounded and who needed intensive care, whose life was in danger, after being taken care of surgically and after reanimation, were put in the intensive care unit. They said that they had been taken care of, but they weren't sure whether there were other members of the paramilitary who may have been wounded and that they didn't know where these were. But the ones who came, I think there were seven or eight of them, were given the best professional care, and they were hospitalised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, seven or eight of the Serbs from Borovo Selo were treated as wounded in your hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were you present when they were brought in or did you get involved in their treatment later on?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present when they were brought in. But on my arrival, because they had not all been dealt with immediately, after my return from the Osijek hospital and through the roadblock where I was held up, and I won't tell you all the threats they uttered against me, on my return I started assisting the wounded and looking after them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You are saying that because you had to go through Trpinja on your way back from Osijek you came late, when the wounded were already in hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember or did you check whether the wounded we are discussing now, those seven or eight, were registered in the hospital register?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were all registered with all the diagnoses and records of their treatment and therapy. If one wants to find this information, it has to be sought from the JNA, because when the JNA entered Vukovar Hospital, it removed all the hospital documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Tell me this: The wounded men, were they guarded by the police, or were they without any kind of guard? Did they have the status of detainees; in other words, had they been arrested or not?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They did not have the status of detainees specially, at least to the best of my recollection. There was no special guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were there any armed policemen -- I'm not referring to those who were brought in as wounded; I'm referring to policemen guarding the hospital, policemen in the hospital, at the time, that is the 2nd of May 1991?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no police presence, either in or around the hospital, on the 2nd of May 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And what about the following days? Does the same apply, in May 1991?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, and I cannot tell you whether a policeman came to the hospital to inquire about someone who was wounded, and who came to visit someone.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: To visit or to question? Did you have situations where the police came to question your patients?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. When I said that they were in intensive care, and that's where they were put, no visitors were allowed, as far as civilians are concerned, either before or after the event you are asking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Certainly no one is allowed to visit an intensive care unit. However, once they were taken out of the intensive care unit, would policemen then come and question people?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, at least no one asked me for permission to go and question somebody. I assume it would have been proper for either myself or Dr. Ivankovic, who was partly responsible for the surgical ward, to be asked permission for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you recall what happened later on with these wounded? Was their treatment successful? Were they discharged? Do you remember what happened to them afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, they all recovered well. They regained their health. Some were almost completely cured, because wounds from various military weapons, whether explosives or bullets, sometimes take much longer to treat than other kinds of wounds. So I cannot say they were completely cured, but as far as I can recall, they were exchanged for some, as I heard, captured Croatian policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Njavro, that they did have the status of detainees after all, not just your patients?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't put it like that, because the policemen in their own country, if they have not committed a crime, cannot be considered to be detainees, if there is no court order and no proper decision issued by the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I understand that. But it's a fact, isn't it, as you said yourself, that they were exchanged. Therefore, that means that their status was not that of citizens who were completely free and able to go wherever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps one of the reasons was that this was -- and I'm only putting this forward as a possibility because, as I say, I am not really competent to comment on this, but I couldn't accept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. After that day and that event, can you tell me whether there was a sudden departure of Serbs from their jobs from the town of Vukovar? Did they fail to show up for work and abandon their jobs? Do you remember the situation in the Vukovar Hospital in this respect?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that both Serbs and non-Serbs left the hospital. Serbs, Croats and people of other ethnicities. It wasn't just Serbs who did that. And if someone was afraid, it wasn't just members of a single ethnic group. Fear was not characteristic of only one of the ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell me or give me an example of any Croat stopping coming to work or resigning from their jobs in the hospital Vukovar? Were they feeling threatened or did this apply only to Serbs, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that anybody had reason to feel threatened. The best indicator of that is that all of those Serbs who remained in the hospital were not harmed in any way, and any suffering they had to endure was shared by all of us. Everybody had the same treatment. Everybody was threatened in the same way, threatened by shelling, destruction. We all suffered equally all the misery of war, they and us Croats who worked at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I understand your answer. It is clear that all of those who remained at work shared the same destiny. But my question is this: The fear and the inability to reach their workplaces due to roadblocks, did it perhaps influence Serbs and make them leave the area and their jobs?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so. I can give you an example from Borovo Selo. A woman was married to the son of priest Zarko from one of the surrounding villages, and she would come to work without any problems every day. In addition to that, there were people who would come from Brsadin and other surrounding areas and had no trouble reaching their work. On the other hand, Croats who lived in Brsadin and Borovo Selo and in that area were unable to move about freely, whereas the Serbs living there and employed at the medical centre and Vukovar Hospital had freedom of movement. There was no reason for that fear. It's quite another matter if somebody left on their own, of their own free will. Yes, there was some Croat doctors who left the Vukovar Hospital as well as nurses. And there were Serbs who did the same thing. Therefore, national background can be no justification for feeling threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. That is your conclusion that these two things were not related. It is solely your opinion. Now that we've touched upon these roadblocks, tell me this, please: Borovo Naselje is close by. It is between Borovo Selo and Vukovar. Can we agree that it was predominantly populated by Croats?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Borovo Naselje, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were there any roadblocks erected there that somebody who wanted to go from Borovo Selo to Vukovar had to pass through, like that example of the woman you gave us?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once they started erecting roadblocks on the other side, these roadblocks on the Croat side did not hinder passage from Borovo Selo to work or even to the Borovo factory while it still operated, but in the reverse direction it was impossible to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can you tell us how you learned this? How come you know this?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know this from the nurse who worked there. She was the nurse in charge of surgical instruments. She was my assistant during surgeries, and she told me this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But if she for any reason was able to pass through, as a woman, do you think that men from Borovo Selo were allowed through as well, especially if they were believed to be Chetniks, as you told us? Do you think they were able to pass through Borovo Naselje and the roadblocks erected there?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that anybody in Vukovar believed all Serbs from Borovo Selo or anywhere else to be Chetniks. Therefore, I can't say that for that reason passage was hindered to everybody going through the roadblocks. I'm just telling you what I know, what I was told. I never spent any time at that roadblock in order to monitor who was allowed through, who wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember at the time, during the period before the 2nd of May, 1991, and especially later, were there any frequent explosions? Were houses blown up, kiosks? Did this happen in Vukovar and the hinterland?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that. I lived in Vukovar near the downtown area and the hospital, because the hospital is very close to the downtown area. I heard those stories. There were explosions. However, it was said and believed that it had been done by certain individuals leaving Vukovar for reasons known only to them. They didn't want the houses to go in anybody else's hands. Or perhaps they wanted to collect money from insurance, because the house had been insured prior to that. This is what I heard from the insurance company which are still in operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, is that consistent with what you told us about tensions? You said that tensions were not palpable, and how come these houses were blown up, even if somebody was indeed leaving Vukovar, why would they blow their own house up? Is that an indicator of the disrupted inter-ethnic relations?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, quite the opposite. It means that the extreme elements, who always caused trouble, did this in order to provoke hatred and lack of tolerance. As you know, they didn't succeed in this aim because once Vukovar was occupied, a large number of Serbs found themselves under siege. These Serbs did not want to leave because they felt they hadn't done anything bad and there was no reason for them to leave, and they suffered the same misery everybody else did. They lived in basements, underground, like moles. They lived just like everybody else did and suffered identically.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My question doesn't pertain to that. I asked you about these explosions and cases of buildings blown up. Do you know that the Borba kiosk, which sold Borba newspaper printed in Belgrade, was blown up?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any specific facility that was blown up. I didn't pay attention to that. I as a doctor, as a human being, had to calm down the tensions. As I've told you, I spent practically 24 hours a day in the hospital. Those who came to me, who needed medical attention, would, in passing, tell me these stories, that people were blowing up their own houses for those two reasons that I just gave you. They didn't come to me to tell me these stories. They came because they needed medical attention and in passing told me this. I, for my part, didn't go around to verify this because I had other things to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that you heard this. Did you hear complaints that this was a type of pressure applied and that as a result of this pressure, people were leaving those settlements which had a mixed population?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was precisely the settlements populated predominantly by Croats that lost most of their residents. It didn't happen in town because otherwise everybody would have left Vukovar, and it is incredible that those Serbs who lived there didn't leave the town despite the terrible damage that Vukovar suffered when the JNA and paramilitary Chetnik formations inflicted pain and suffering on the entire city every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, I'm now referring to the time period before the shelling, immediately before and after the 2nd of May, 1991. Let us please focus on that period of time, and we will reach other topics that you mentioned later on. Before the break, let's turn to several other issues from this period of time. Were you able to see another kind of pressure exerted upon Serbs in Vukovar, namely were the Vukovar Serbs removed in large number from offices that they held in various enterprises, institutions and even your hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you about the situation in the hospital. As for the other institutions, it was up to political parties to appoint people to offices. This is the system that was in place after multi-party elections, when the new democratic methods were applied, those accepted else where in the world. As for the Vukovar Hospital, I can tell you something about these replacements. They were not replacements. They were cases of people resigning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: These resignations, were they forced? Were they required to resign?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't describe it that way. I think that this kind of change was needed even prior to that. Why? Once the Borovo Selo event happened, once the Croatian policemen were killed in Borovo Selo, the then director of the Vukovar medical centre refused to send ambulances with appropriate medical teams to provide assistance there. Medically speaking, I will try to use moderate terms here, but this could be termed as medical negligence. Later on, certain Croats and certain Serbs left on their own without seeking legally available options, meaning they did not use their annual leaves or sick leaves and so on, but, rather, left their jobs upon receiving authorisation from the then director, which was not legal. You as a lawyer know that there used to be the law on labour, which set forth the cases in which somebody had to be fired when they failed to show up for work without justification. Since there were many such cases, there were requests to apply the law. Once this was made known, I believe that it was quite natural for the then director to suffer consequences of his illegal work, and as a result of that, the director resigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I agree with you that failure to show up at work was one of the reasons for firing somebody, both in Croatia and in the former Yugoslavia. Do you believe that under those emergency circumstances, he perhaps wanted to help these people to preserve something as valuable as a job, hoping that better times would come?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be correct if it weren't for the others who remained there precisely in order to protect their jobs. Those who left left because they didn't want to suffer. They wanted to avoid the misery that came with working under emergency circumstances, and they, as medical professionals, should not be allowed to do that. They violated their professional roles, and I believe it was quite normal for them to suffer legal consequences as was normal for the director to resign.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The resignation, based on everything you said, was not a voluntary one but, rather, the director was forced to resign. However, not because he was a Serb but, rather, for all these other reasons that you enumerated. If that is indeed the case, tell us this: Do you know that the Serbs were removed from all other leading top offices except for the public audit agency? For example, the factory in Borovo, MUP and so on.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the direct -- the then director of the medical centre was not a Serb but, rather, a Montenegrin. That's the first thing I wanted to say. Second, in 1972 and earlier, a lot of Croats were removed from offices and nobody made any trouble on that account. Whoever comes to an office should be valued based on their contribution, regardless of what ethnic community they belong to. You said that these people were replaced because they were Serbs, but what is interesting, that it was precisely the Serbs who occupied these prestigious offices. And there was this policy of ethnic quotas that was applied in Vukovar, and it's a bit strange, bearing in mind everything else that happened prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that this is a convenient time for the break, if you agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. We will resume sitting at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, somehow or other you must be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Njavro, one day before the event we have discussed at length, of the 2nd of May, that is, on the 1st of May 1991, do you remember admitting as an urgent case, Stefan Inic [phoen] from Brsadin who had been wounded with a bullet?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I do remember receiving Ljubica Nemcic also shot in Brsadin. She and her husband had been on their way to Vinkovci to collect their son. She was brought to hospital with a serious injury to her lower leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you know Mrs. Danica Grojic, a teacher?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Have you heard that on the 31st of May, 1991, while she was at the window, shots were fired at her house?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I would probably have heard about it because she lived close to my mother-in-law, almost in the same street.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Were shots often heard in Vukovar by day and by night in that period?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I spent most of my time in the hospital. I was always either at the ward with patients or in the outpatients' clinic examining patients who had appointments, and this took place both in the morning and afternoon and in the evening. So I could neither know nor hear, when I was in the basement, whether any shots could be heard in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One more question about this. I may already have asked you about explosions in houses, but I haven't mentioned restaurants and cafes, so I will read out a few names of restaurants and cafes owned by Serbs which were blown up in April or May. Tell me whether you know any of them or have heard of any of them. Krajisnik in April 1991?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't even know where it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Sarajka?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajka was a cafe near the market in Vukovar. Its owner was -- at least that's what I heard, because people who came to the hospital later, when there were already operations going on, people told me that he had been an extreme nationalist and chauvinist and that allegedly he himself blew up his cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: He was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We are discussing Sarajka. I think it doesn't say that in the transcript. On the 3rd of May, only a day after what happened in Borovo Selo, on the same day, the cafe called Tufo; do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know where it was or if it existed. I don't doubt that it existed because you say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The cafe Brdo on the 6th of May, the Serb holiday of Djurdjevdan?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that because I would often go to visit friends on the 6th. My name is Juraj, and they would invite me to a celebration.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But you don't know about this cafe?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mali Raj cafe, blown up on Vidovdan, the 28th of June, St. Vitus Day?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you, sir, that I was not a man who frequented cafes, so I wouldn't know what kind of people went to what cafes, and I couldn't really say anything about any cafes, apart from Sarajka, which I know because my mother-in-law used to go to the market. That's why I know where it is. But for the others, hardly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I won't go on then. There are nine on my list that were blown up in a month and a half but I'll put that aside and move on. You certainly know that in Vukovar there was a barracks of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time, in May and June and later, there were efforts to hinder the work of the barracks, to block the barracks, to cut off water and electricity and to make it impossible for the barracks to operate?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I do know that in front of the hospital, I saw APCs passing by with rotating weapons, and individual soldiers would raise three fingers and this could have been seen as a provocation by some, especially Croats. Sometimes you would hear them singing songs which were not typical folk songs but, on the contrary, were provocative. During one such APC ride, or a ride in a vehicle, some soldiers were injured and were brought to the hospital where they were given assistance. I think their commander was Captain Curcin or Curcic. He thanked me for the treatment of those soldiers. A day or two later, they were moved to the military medical academy in Belgrade. The soldiers themselves told me they had been transporting weapons. I didn't ask them about it because I wasn't interested at the time to Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm not interested in it either, so please try to focus on my question. My question was about the barracks in Vukovar. Do you know that it was obstructed in the ways I have described and finally blocked?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not until sometime in August, when I learned that - and that was towards the end of August - that the barracks were being blocked and that water and electricity had been cut off because the town was being destroyed from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You are speaking of the end of August?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But more than one witness said that this started on the 24th or the 25th of August. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovar was shelled even prior to that. My flat, which is close to the hospital, was damaged on the 6th of August, 1991. Everybody told me that the shell came from the barracks, the barracks was at Sajmiste. I am not familiar with different types of military weapons used to launch shells.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. In answer to a question put by my learned friend Mr. Moore about the 6th of August, you said this. I was asking you about the 25th. Is that the real date when the shelling of Vukovar started or no? Between the 6th and the 25th, were there any such events?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Vukovar was shelled prior to that. In Borovo Naselje - I said Borovo Selo; I meant to say Borovo Naselje - there was destruction there. After the 6th, there was a shell that landed on the 13th of August. Shells landed not only close to the hospital. One landed close to the hospital on the 6th of August, and the operating theatre at the surgical ward was badly damaged. And then on that same day, a shell landed in the crown of a tree in front of the window of my flat, and fortunately the tree prevented the shell from entering the apartment. The town was also shelled on the 13th. Among other places, a shell landed in the park where there was a building where JNA officers resided. That building was hit. After that, there was heavy shelling, as you said, sir, starting on the 24th onward. It then became relentless and on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know that after the 24th of August a JNA plane was shot down above Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because even before that, JNA planes had bombed the villages around Vukovar and Vukovar itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So your answer is yes, you know of this?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you know who shot the plane down?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A member of the National Guard Corps shot down the plane, but with what? I'm really not familiar with weapons, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now that we mention the National Guard Corps, Mr. Njavro, you said more than once that you kept records in the hospital as to whether a patient was a member of the Croatian police or of the ZNG. This was specially registered. My question is: What is the National Guard Corps?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am no military expert and I was not a minister of the police. I was not the one who organised either the police or the National Guard Corps. So that I cannot give you a precise definition. I do know that it was an integral part of the police forces and that it was under the competence of the Ministry of the Interior, that is, the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it a military formation placed under the Ministry of the Interior because Croatia did not have an army? If you agree with me, the only army was the JNA at the time because the state of Yugoslavia still existed.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think it was a guard attached to the police of the kind that exist in other countries. It was a police formation known as the National Guard Corps of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Wasn't it a paramilitary formation, in view of the way it was established and its composition?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If it went through all the regular legal procedures needed in such cases, it was passed through parliament and approved by the government, as is usually done in all democratic countries which have this form, this combination of police and guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it possible, regardless of whose decision it was, in view of the existence of the federal state and the army and the way the state functioned at the time, and let me remind you that at that time the Republic of Croatia had not been separated from Yugoslavia or at least did not have that kind of recognition?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly, it was or, rather, certainly it existed because there was a Presidency of sorts. There was the government of Ante Markovic. But Croatia as an independent Socialist Republic of the then federal state legally, at least to the best of my knowledge, because law is not my field, did have the possibility legally to have a National Guard Corps, not a paramilitary formation but regular police forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What uniforms did they wear? The military camouflage uniforms or the blue police uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore for the most part, at the outset, as far as I can recall, of course, both uniforms. In such operations, this is probably worn because wherever I see special police forces, I see them wearing camouflage uniforms, so I wouldn't be surprised by the fact that the guard had those uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. But the colours of the camouflage uniforms are different. You mentioned Mr. Ante Markovic as the then Prime Minister of the federal government. He was a Croat, was he not?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask him for his nationality. I don't know. I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I didn't ask him either, but I think it's a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely. He was a member of Croatian nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember who at that time, time period relevant for Vukovar, was the president of Yugoslavia, of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I know which period of time you're referring to, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: From July onwards.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: From July onwards, no. I know, though, that there was a lot of tension regarding that. It was the turn of Croatia to appoint its member to be president of the Presidency, and it was supposed to be Mr. Stipe Mesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did Mr. Stipe Mesic become president of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I think that it was the sunset of that system. I think that the authorities of Stipe Mesic were more of a formal protocol kind of nature and that he was unable to influence in any real way the events unfolding in the then Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that Mr. Stipe Mesic became president of the Presidency on the 1st of July, 1991, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would. I would. You must know this better than I do, being a lawyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Another issue concerning his nationality, I hope that we will agree that he was and still is a Croat and is the current president of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Now I would like to turn to another issue concerning the hospital. We spoke about the surgery ward before these events occurred, or rather before you were appointed head of the war medical services. Who was the head nurse of the surgical ward?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Mrs. Binazija Kolesar, licensed nurse.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did she remain there in the hospital to the end in that role as head nurse?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You most probably knew her well because you had worked together. Can you tell us whether she is a person you could trust, somebody who did their job well?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that she was a conscientious worker, selfless and performed her job of head nurse of the surgical ward in the most humane and professional manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you believe that she is the kind of person who would have no reason to utter anything that wasn't true about the events that unfolded during that period of time at the Vukovar Hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, since you asked me about inter-ethnic relations elsewhere and in the hospital, please allow me to say that as far as I know, although I do not -- I never asked Mrs. Kolesar this, but I think that she was married to a Ruthenian and that she herself is a Bosniak or something to that effect. She is not a Croat. Therefore, she did not let her national feelings come through in her work. She performed her work conscientiously, professionally, and I believe that her attitude during her testimony here had to be identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you spoke about the records kept in the hospital, register books, diagnoses and all other particulars that were entered in those books, you said that especially after May 1991, in addition to general information, the affiliation of a patient was also recorded, whether he was a member of MUP, ZNG or a civilian. But was the nationality of a patient also recorded?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not in a single case. I can assure you of this. It did not even occur to anybody to record the nationality of patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. My next question, then, is this: Based on what were you able to know the nationality of patients? Very often we heard percentages discussed here, percentages of patients of this nationality or that nationality. Therefore, based on what were you able to establish that, if this was not recorded?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to give me some specific examples because I never uttered such things. When the patients arrived in the hospital, those who were from Vukovar and whom I knew - sometimes I knew entire families - then yes, I would know the nationality of those patients because I would attend various family or religious holidays and celebrations in their houses. I knew what customs they followed. Therefore, it was not difficult at all to know their nationality. However, that never affected -- we never allowed that to affect our attitude. This applied to the entire medical staff. It was quite another matter when members of the JNA came in as patients, who were wounded or perhaps members of paramilitary formations. In those cases, they would say themselves, even though we never required that, that they were Serbs, for example, and that they didn't join the army or the formation of their own will but were, rather, mobilised, and this is how we knew about the nationality of the patients.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you believe -- you told us that some of them said that they had been mobilised, forced to join the military and so on. Do you believe that they expected some problems to arise in the hospital and this is why they felt it necessary to declare this to you?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later on, after they received treatment, after they relaxed and saw how we treated them, then they would say this to us, because prior to arriving in the hospital they had been terrified. They had been told all kinds of stories, that they would be killed, mutilated and so on, upon arriving in the hospital. Therefore, it was quite natural for them, quite human of them, to declare voluntarily how they did not join the army of their own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We mentioned some soldiers who were patients in the hospital. You mentioned this in examination-in-chief, specifically Sasa Jovic. I would like to ask you whether you remember Ivan Zivkovic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that Ivan Zivkovic was also seriously wounded, that he recovered, and I wouldn't be able to say but I believe that he joined the National Guards Corps. However, I'm not positive about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: He was a Serb?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did you know Tomo Jakovljevic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tomo Jakovljevic used to work as a plaster technician. He was a very good one. He did his job well, although he wasn't properly trained. Rather, during his military service, he served as a male nurse, and this is where he learned how to work with plaster. He was quite skillful. He lived in Leva Supoderica. He said that he had been injured by the JNA shell. I think that either his left or right leg was injured. Unfortunately, he was left unassisted for some two or three days, and then the members of the ZNG found him all alone in a semi-destroyed house, and they brought him to the hospital where he received treatment and where unfortunately we had to amputate his leg before -- below the knee. One day he was almost, once again, injured by a shell which fell above him and injured him slightly. Since the hospital was full of seriously injured persons, he and some other wounded were transferred to Borovo Komerc where there was a safer shelter and perhaps even more comfort, better living circumstances. I know that he was transferred there. What happened to Tomo Jakovljevic afterwards, I don't know, because those of us who remained in the Vukovar Hospital were overworked. We had sent orthopaedists and other specialists to Borovo Komerc to ensure that those who were half recovered, those who no longer needed surgical assistance but still needed some medical attention were receiving medical care. Those who did not have life-threatening wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. So you don't know what happened to them afterwards?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember a soldier Nedeljko Turukalo?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you remember soldier Slavomir Bestin?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Milan Biber?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I know that various soldiers who had been abandoned by their own forces, soldiers of the JNA and paramilitary members, Chetniks, were also brought to the hospital, and under the existing circumstances, we gave them our best.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, you said this many times before. Please give the shortest possible answers to my questions. Do you remember soldier Stankovic, Branko?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We treated a lot of soldiers and other members of paramilitary formations as well as JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did anybody guard the soldiers during their hospitalisations, any member of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of potential emotional outbursts, as we had a lot of wounded policemen and ZNG members, in order to prevent any incidents, in order to ensure that nobody wanted to physically settle accounts with the wounded or do something worse to them, we attempted to keep them secluded and thus protected from the MUP members. We wanted to ensure that they had protection, that they received appropriate medical care and that this was provided by only a limited number of nurses. So that we prevented any potential situation, even though it wasn't likely, for any nurse to do something to them. Therefore, certain nurses took care of them, and they were protected by police members. Naturally, I myself visited them regularly. I made hospital rounds. And whatever medication we had, food and all other supplies, we shared with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. You described that at length. My question was: What happened to the people once they recovered? Who took them over?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once people recovered, or rather all people who were gravely wounded, especially in cases of serious, grave injuries, where people had extensive haemorrhage, infections, amputations of extremities where huge amounts of blood supplies were used so that we had none --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I only asked you about the people who recovered.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to complete my thought. I'm telling you how we operated. All of these people need a long-term and multi-month medical attention, so that once the occupational forces and paramilitary formations entered the area, those --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Please restrict yourself to just answering my questions, if possible. Do you know somebody called Damir Samardzic, known as Veliki Bojler?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was he one of those who guarded the soldiers in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes. But he wasn't the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did those persons carry weapons while in hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those persons did not carry weapons while they were in the hospital. Whenever anyone entered the hospital, they had to lay aside their weapons. Only the seriously wounded who were taken by the police to the police station, but there were sometimes armed guards in front of the room where these wounded soldiers were being treated for their own protection, for their own safety. The weapons were pistols or Kalashnikovs. I think that's what they were called.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you aware of an incident that took place on the occasion of a visit to a room where a wounded Croatian policeman was lying, and he pulled out a pistol and pointed it at Dr. Ivankovic because of a word he used to describe him, saying he was a real hero?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. I'm not aware of it. I do, however, remember a previous incident because, in front of his house, two members of the ZNG were killed. They thought --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this incident in the hospital, if you know about it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned that three soldiers, Sasa Jovic and two others, I think, were handed over to the army. What about the other soldiers who were treated before that and I assume cured in your hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, one group was handed over to the military medical academy. Captain Djurdjevic came, as I said, and thanked us for our timely medical assistance to these men, and they were taken, as far as I know, to the military medical academy. Those three that I mentioned and that you are asking me about, Sasa Jovic, Pavle Teofanovic, and Srdjan Miljkovic, were also partially cured, not completely, and handed over to units of the JNA. As for others, I really don't recall either when or at what time they were wounded or when they turned up in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned July; I think it's not in the transcript. That's why I'm taking you back to that, at the beginning of your reply.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand you. Could you please repeat your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you were speaking of Curcin or Curcic, what month was that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that but it didn't enter the transcript. That's why I'm asking you this. Now I'd like to ask you something about the evacuation of seriously wounded people organised in October by the Medecins Sans Frontieres. Who selected the patients, or rather who drew up a list of the patients to be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was doctors who did that. There were urologists there as well. You mentioned only surgeons, but there was an orthopaedist, a urologist. There were wounded who had urological injuries, and they also needed to be transported for further treatment or in order to save their lives. Also an orthopaedic specialist, because of their limbs. There were cases where urgent interventions were need.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. In surgical cases, was it you who selected the patients from your ward who were to be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I knew who were the most serious patients, threatened with serious infections, whose injuries were life-threatening, and who could receive better assistance in better -- better equipped institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But my question was, was it you who drew up the list of those in the surgical ward to be evacuated?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the wounded were in the surgical ward, but the surgery was not just general surgery. There was also urology, orthopaedics, gynaecology, and other various types of injuries, and all of this was under one umbrella, that of surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
