utterances.text: Did you ask for the agreement of those patients? Were they told they were to be evacuated and did they accept it?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly. They could hardly wait because of the shelling of the hospital. The shells were falling down like rain. One couldn't go out. If you went out, you might never come back. They were clutching at straws. And they all agreed to be evacuated for further treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You will recall I asked you about Private Ivan Zivkovic. You said you thought that he had been discharged and joined the ZNG. If I were to tell you that he was among those included in the transport organised by the Medecins Sans Frontieres, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible. But if he was, it was his wish to go with the others because this was offered to him. It only shows that all those who were seriously wounded and given assistance, regardless of what side they belonged to in these horrors of war, were given professional assistance, and they themselves could decide whether they wanted to go or not. He decided he did want to go, and I believe that he did, as you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I told you that, yes, he was in this transport, that's correct, I can hardly accept that he agreed to that and that he was very happy about it, because he managed somehow to attract attention when they were passing by a JNA unit, and he managed to get pulled out because he didn't want to go to Zagreb. The transport was going to Zagreb. Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Everybody knows --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. If you haven't heard about it, there is no need --

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that it was his choice to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: May I just ask to seek clarification in relation to one matter on that topic? If my learned friend is going to be suggesting as part of the Defence case that this particular soldier indicated to this doctor or other doctors that he did not wish to be evacuated, then I would submit that he should put that clearly on the record because what is happening at the moment is the doctor is saying, "I am not aware of that." Then the question is being formulated in a way, well, later on, he protested or that this soldier protested. It is beholden upon the Defence, and indeed the Prosecution when they are putting their case, that they should put specifics to enable a witness and indeed the other side to know exactly what the case is. So if it's being said that this soldier had said specifically to a doctor at the hospital, "I do not wish to be evacuated" and was coerced into so doing, I submit that that should be done at this stage or perhaps before the conclusion of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, you have heard the point. It's a valid one. If it is the Defence case that this patient was protesting against being moved to Zagreb, you should put that to the witness in the course of the cross-examination rather than hedging around the matter, which is the way the questions have been to the present time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I really hope that Ivan Zivkovic will appear before this Court as a Defence witness and will be able to testify about this, because we will not have other witnesses to events taking place in the hospital. We will have witnesses who will testify to the manner in which he managed to leave the convoy evacuating the patients to Zagreb. However, Mr. Njavro said that Ivan Zivkovic joined the ZNG and was discharged. He didn't mention that he was in this convoy, which is why I was paying a little more attention to this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that is your case, Mr. Domazet, you, I believe, should be putting to the witness whether this patient protested about being moved to Zagreb, to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will formulate my question in this manner, although the witness did reply that he wasn't on the list and now he said he was. But I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Witness, do you remember that Ivan Zivkovic did not wish to be sent to Zagreb and opposed this?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert categorically before this Honourable Tribunal that not a single wounded person who was taken by the Medecins Sans Frontieres in the convoy from the Vukovar Hospital on the 19th of September left the hospital against his will. Each one was asked whether he wished to go. It was well known where they would be going: For further medical treatment in Croatia. After they agreed, they were taken outside and put in the ambulances and then they could proceed on their way. As for what I said, that he joined the guards, it's true that there was an Ivan Zivkovic who did join the ZNG. I may have been confused about which Ivan Zivkovic it was. He came from the JNA. Maybe it was another Ivan Zivkovic and not this one, but I assert categorically that he was asked in the hospital, "Do you want the Medecins Sans Frontieres to take you in a convoy to the free part of Croatia for further medical treatment?" Each and every patient, after he agreed to this, could continue his road to further treatment by the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Mr. Njavro, when speaking about Private Ivan Zivkovic, a Serb soldier, you said that he had been almost cured, and you felt that he -- you thought that he had joined the ZNG. But you said just a while ago here that only the most seriously wounded patients were included in this convoy. Was he really as seriously wounded or was he about to be discharged? Why was he sent to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I described how the triage was carried out. I did not conduct the triage for each patient personally, so I cannot answer with respect to each and every individual. Even had I done so, it would be impossible to remember 112 names - I think it was 112 - of patients who were taken from the Vukovar Hospital by the Medecins Sans Frontieres. Maybe not you personally but I believe that everybody knows the hardships suffered by these patients on their way to Zagreb to undergo further medical treatment, and wounded people died en route.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that, yes. During the examination-in-chief, you did say that the trip took a long time, that they travelled across fields, didn't use the normal roads. How did you come by this information? Because the convoy was supposed to take a safe route.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received information because every hour or two we asked about this. We called Zagreb and asked, because Luzac, Bogdanovci, Marinci, Zidine, Nustar, Vinkovci, the route that was supposed to be used, even if you drove very slowly, because these people were wounded, it wouldn't take more than two hours. However, when we called, because we had a telephone communication with Zagreb, when we asked whether the wounded people had arrived and what the situation was, the answer was no, which gave rise to concern and even panic. We thought it might have been better to keep them in hospital than --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said that, Mr. Njavro, but I'm asking you whether you had information even if there was a detour, on whose initiative did it happen? Was it those who were in charge of the convoy that caused the detour?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information I received, because I didn't know then why that convoy had taken so long to arrive, but there was a member of the intelligence services, Mr. Zvonko Markovic or Mihajlovic, whom General Raseta sent to escort the convoy, told the whole story, the whole course of events, and what was done to hold back the convoy, even when it fell into mud in a field, they had to pull it out. They wanted to hold it up for as long as possible, and my impression was that this was done in order to make the situation of the wounded patients worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That is a very serious allegation. That's why I'm asking you on whose initiative the convoy left the road and took a route through the meadows.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The initiative came from members of the JNA because after the convoy passed through Luzac, they met it and told it to take the field road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Iffy to tell you that there was no JNA at Luzac and that this was Croatian territory and that the JNA forces were much further away waiting for the convoy which before that had left the road, would you agree with me or do you have other information?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I wouldn't agree with you. I do not wish to contradict you but I certainly know this area better than you do. I crossed it many times. Therefore, Luzac is not only the settlement itself but before -- once you cross the bridge, and get to the road for Bogdanovci, then it is the area after that, through the fields, where what I have just described to you took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. I will not dwell on this topic any longer. Let us turn back to the hospital. It is well known -- and you also told us -- that the hospital did not have electrical supply after a certain period of time and that it was forced to use generators. What did the generators supply? Just one area of the hospital or the entire hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to go down in the basement in early August, on the 6th of August to be precise, when the operating room was destroyed. There was a risk that the shelling would continue, so in order to ensure safety for the patients, we took them down to the basement for several days and then took them up again, and then after that brought them in the basement again. As for the electrical outage, it certainly started happening in September, and in October we had no more electrical supply whatsoever, not only in the hospital but in town as well. We had generators. They supplied only the vital section. We needed to procure fuel for generators - we didn't have a lot of fuel - and had access only to whatever was left at gas stations. We used that for a time to cover only the vital operations in the hospital, surgeries, bandages, sterilisation of equipment and instruments that were necessary to perform surgical interventions, labours and so on. We also had to have sterile material for bandages and so on. We had no water either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That was not my question. And you have answered my question. If I understood you well, you said that the generators were used only for the vital work at the hospital, surgeries, sterilisation of equipment and so on.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean that generators were not used to supply electricity for lights, for offices of doctors and so on?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that we used candles in the offices because one could still find candles in town. As for the exact description of precisely which lights were supplied by the generator and which weren't, I don't remember. However, I do remember that in the last several days, on the 17th and 18th of November, I performed a surgery on a three-year-old girl --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, you told us about that in examination-in-chief. Let us now please focus on the questions that I have. What was the situation like in relation to telephone lines of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only telephone connection out of the hospital was the telephone in the office of Dr. Bosanac. One could regularly talk to Zagreb and the area around. I think it was also possible to talk to other cities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Until which time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last time we were able to use the phone, if I remember well, was on the 17th in the evening. Or perhaps the 18th in the morning. I'm not sure. But one of those two days was the last day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: 17th or 18th of what?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That means until the very end, while you were still at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was just on the last day that we had no telephone connection, the 19th or the 20th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Based on what you said, it seems that you frequently went to the office of your director, Mrs. Bosanac; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not just I, but anybody who needed went into the office of Dr. Bosanac. If they needed to ask for something. Otherwise, unfortunately I spent most of my time in the operating room, or in one of the improvised operating rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me just correct something that is missing in the transcript. You said that there was no telephone connections starting on the 18th in the afternoon and then on the 19th and 20th. The 18th in the afternoon is not mentioned in the transcript. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was either on the 17th or the 18th that we used the phone for the last time, but I don't remember that. You need to ask Dr. Bosanac that because she was the one who used the phone line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. Since you entered that office, do you remember what items were in that office of Dr. Bosanac?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The usual. The documentation, medical histories. Nothing remarkable. I don't remember seeing anything unusual there. Oh, yes, the salaries. The salaries were there, in a sack, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You didn't see anything else?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The cigarettes, while we still had them. I don't remember anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, in relation to this time period that you just mentioned, which is the period immediately preceding the arrival of the JNA in the hospital, was there an increase in the number of those coming to the hospital, including those who had no injuries whatsoever, or were not sick?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given that on the 16th, the shelling ceased, the shelling and the destruction, the 17th was a Sunday, and on that day people started leaving basements and the whole town of Vukovar and came to the hospital. Prior to that, they spent 70 to 80 days in the basements. They came to the hospital hoping to find salvation there, hoping to find safety there. I have to say that in the building where I lived, below my flat was a basement, where almost all remaining residents stayed, and all of them, they came to the hospital on the 17th in the afternoon, including my wife, my mother-in-law, and they came there to wait, because they had heard, they had been warned, that the paramilitary Chetnik formations, and even the JNA, were conducting cleansing of the buildings. They were throwing bombs into the basements and inquiring whether anybody survived and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: All right. Please concentrate on my question. So your answer was yes, civilians came to the hospital too. My question was whether the members of the ZNG came seeking shelter, or seeking a way to leave Vukovar via the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm trying to explain how it came about that the hospital was so full. I said that the hospital was so full that it could not admit another person. As for the members of the ZNG, I do not believe that they were there. Because on the 18th some of them surrendered at Mitnica. And the others, with the then commander of the Vukovar defence, Mladi Jastreb, went to attempt a breakthrough. Now, whether it's possible that some of the members of the ZNG entered the hospital as civilians, perhaps there were some such individual cases, but it wasn't anything on such a scale as to be noticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't know whether this is an appropriate time for a break or should I carry on?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I think that would be an ideal time for a break. We will resume at five minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Would Your Honour hear me just on one small matter?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's to do with the next witness, Ambassador Okun. He has testified in the Milosevic case. He relied on his original document, his diary. He wishes to use that document again for his evidence, which I hope will be tomorrow. We have moved heaven and earth but not the Registry to obtain the original document. And the ambassador is justifiably concerned that the morning of trial he still hasn't got access to the original document. We even filed a motion on, I think, Friday, to obtain this document. I don't know if the Court would be able, of its own motion, to be able to assist the Prosecution. But the last thing we need is a delay to try and obtain a document that is being held by the Registry and a document in the Milosevic case as an original but a document that clearly needs to be used in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is any reason being offered for the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There is no reason being given, and there is no reply being given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will make inquiries, Mr. Moore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, the matter you raised before the break, the information the Chamber has received indicates a timetable and a progress of e-mails a little different from your understanding, and the most recent was a specific request to be able to view the diary tomorrow morning and that has been implemented by the Registry. Their general problem is that the document is in their custody by order of another Trial Chamber so that any viewing of it needs to be in their presence. So it would appear that it will be available to you and the witness tomorrow morning at the time requested by one of your people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I think my timetable was correct. We have made requests for access to the original document because Ambassador Okun would like to see his document. He is 82 years of age, and he would like to see his document in preparation of giving evidence. I accept that there has been an arrangement made for tomorrow morning but that has been what I will call a fallback position because we have not been able to have access to the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The answer to that, as I anticipate where it's leading, would have been to seek an order from the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we've done that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Have you got the order from the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I believe that -- may I just check, because I know that there was a motion -- a motion laid before the Court from the Milosevic team, if I may use that phrase, for the document, for the release of the document. May I just clarify one matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. I certainly sought on my e-mail, I think either Friday or this morning, on Friday, and if it can be turned upped but my case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is no point in approaching this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your problem is an order of another Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that is in your way, you need to get that order varied by that Trial Chamber, and by what you say, you have commenced steps in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But from what you say you have not yet got that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: No. We made an application in written form in the proper procedure and we have received no reply. But the problem I have is really just a sensible realistic problem of a witness wanting to see his original document when he's giving evidence. It's not an unreasonable stance to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I well understand that, and I would expect the other Trial Chamber would see it as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Well, we'll see tomorrow morning anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: When they come to be formally approached in the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But you understand we can't presume to vary their order. All we can do consistently with their order is to ensure that the witness can see the document in the custody of a court -- or in the presence of a court officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I understand that fully. But sometimes witnesses don't feel, with the utmost courtesy to the members of the Registry present, do not always feel confident or comfortable with a member sitting beside them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore, I'm not questioning that, but that's as far as we can go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We have done that. It's up to you, with the other Trial Chamber, if you want to go further.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Njavro, in examination-in-chief, as well as today, you said that proceedings had been instituted against you before the military court in Belgrade but that you were exchanged. Is it true that you were exchanged prior to commencement of any trial in that military court?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The trial did commence in the high military court in Belgrade. After the hearing was held, I was exchanged. It involved a group of spies called Labrador from Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In order to be fully certain, this is not your area of expertise but rather mine. So were you referring to the investigation? Was it then that you gave your statement? Or was an indictment issued and did the trial actually commence, or were you perhaps just referring to the investigation?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was referring to the trial held in the Belgrade high military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If that is the case, there is no reason we should not believe you that the trial did commence. However, the trial was not concluded, and before it concluded, you were exchanged?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the trial was concluded, but I never received a judgement because after the trial was concluded, I was exchanged, as I have told you, for a spy group from Zagreb called Labrador.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I remember well, that was the spy group arrested in Zagreb and exchanged for the group in which you were, and if I'm not mistaken, you travelled on a plane from Belgrade to Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were 40 or so of us on the plane, us who were -- who had been arrested and kept in prison or camp. There were also some JNA officers travelling with us. When we arrived in Zagreb, when we landed at Pleso airport, we were exchanged there for this Labrador spy group. They entered the plane that we disembarked from, that we had arrived in from Belgrade, from Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You've just said that with you in this group that was exchanged, there were several JNA officers. Do you remember whether General Aleksander Vasiljevic was among them?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a general and the colonel and the wife of, if I recall this correctly, of one of the colonels, commanders at the Pleso airport. Whether this was General Vasiljevic or not, I could not confirm, but there was a general, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And, of course, he returned with this Labrador group; correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say that. We got on a bus and we were taken towards the part of the Pleso airport where the civilian traffic went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In this group that was with you, was Dr. or Mrs. Vesna Bosanac as well in the group?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking is that she mentioned that General Vasiljevic was on the plane, and I thought that perhaps you knew something about this as well.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know that there was a general. I know that -- I remember the rank, but whether this was actually General Vasiljevic or not, I could not categorically confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you agree with the views of some that it was Dr. Vesna Bosanac who was a symbol of Vukovar in the public opinion, especially in the Croatian -- in the eye of the Croatian public opinion, especially because of the events in that area?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Vesna Bosanac was a symbol because she was the one who issued warnings to everyone and warned everyone about what was happening there. She spoke with General Raseta and she pleaded for the destruction of Vukovar to cease and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, my question was -- please answer my question yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you could call it that, because of the appeals that she voiced, especially because she was from Vukovar, then no wonder that she was more in the public eye than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: More than you yourself?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think I am not -- I'm not mistaken but you will tell me if that's so. You said today at the beginning that you were not politically active, that you were never a member of any political party, and that you wouldn't even know what party your mayor belonged to. A few months following this exchange, in other words in the summer of 1992, you became the minister of health in Mr. Sarinic's government, and as far as I know, that was a HDZ government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know, sir, why you would make a link between my engagement in this later on, because it was normal for people in the medical profession to be ministers of health or to be in the health ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Certainly. But you yourself said when you mentioned some appointments to high offices, when I asked you about the names, you said that the political party which would come to power would bring their own people, this was normal, and if I recall correctly, you mentioned that this is how the most responsible people from Vukovar were removed.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I did not say that. I said it was normal procedure, but I didn't say it was a rule. If it was common, or usual, that's how it was. But then again I have to say that in 1991 I was not a member of any party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yeah. But we are talking about 1992, not long after that. Am I correct in saying that sometime after that, up to 1994, you were in this position and then you remained minister at large and were involved with the issues of immigrants and victims of the patriotic war? Am I correct? Is this information correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in 1992, the war was still raging, and there were still atrocities being committed, and it is normal that someone who had experienced and lived through the hell of war and who was also in a camp and was a doctor as well and well acquainted with the health issues, it was normal that such a person would be appointed to an area which he was familiar with and where he had some expertise. And this is why I became minister of health in August of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. In other words, you were appointed to this position even without being a member of any political party. But could that be true for being -- in other words, were you a member of parliament in three sessions?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was elected in 1992, and 1995, and in 2000. In other words, I served during three sessions of parliament, and for a while I was minister of health, after which I was minister at large, but because there were so many immigrants after the aggression against Croatia and then the aggression against Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was a neighbouring country, by the JNA, I was in charge of taking care of the immigrants and refugees from the -- that neighbouring country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that to say that you were elected as member of parliament in three sessions and that you were not a member of any party?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I became a member of the -- in nineteen-ninety -- in the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I understand now, because I understand that you can be appointed to a ministerial post without being a member of a party but you cannot be a member of parliament; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. You can also be an independent. In other words, you can be elected as an independent candidate. You do not necessarily have to belong to a political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that, what you said earlier, that in 1992 you became a member of the HDZ because this is something that was omitted in the transcript. So could you please confirm that for the transcript? In other words, there are independent candidates, that's correct, but you were not independent, you were a member of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I was on the list of candidates of the HDZ, as I said, when I joined the party, which is when I joined the party, and was -- and became its member.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. And this was a very quick career, political career, and if I am not mistaken, you are still a member of the Association of Croatian doctors?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do I recall correctly that you mentioned Jastreb and that you were then -- subsequent to that that you were arrested when the Croatian authorities arrested Jastreb Dedakovic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that, but he was the commander of the Vukovar defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: May I just remind you of the two doctors you mentioned earlier, Serb doctors, Dr. Ivankovic and Dr. Djurinac [phoen]. For the first you said that he was as a member of the League of Communists, the one-time League of Communists, that that's how he was actually appointed and had a privileged position that he also was able to procure a piece of land; and for the other man you said that he was an alcoholic. You never mentioned another colleague. Was there any other colleague that you can recall who was a Serb of whom you would have a positive opinion?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for colleagues, Djurinac, I do not know any such man. I do know Dr. Djuranac. He's in Zagreb, and he's a Croat, unless he changed his nationality in the meantime. And I did not say that he was an alcoholic. I just said that he liked to take a drink or two from time to time. As for other colleagues, I never stated of any of them, nor did I have any reason to, anything that was not true. This would be against my ethics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to go back to my question having to do with Jastreb Dedakovic, and I believe that the transcript does not exactly reflect what you have said. So could you please repeat whether you know that they were arrested and if you know why, tell us why.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that, I know that they were arrested, but why, I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. This is not -- this was not reflected in the transcript. But thank you any way, Mr. Njavro. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Domazet. Yes, Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening, Your Honours. My name is Borivoj Borovic, and I am the Defence counsel for Miroslav Radic. This is for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: To clarify completely the question related to the military court in Belgrade, the first question: How many statements did you make before this Court?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly at this point. I know I was taken --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. We are wasting a lot of time on lengthy questions and lengthy answers, so could you please just answer briefly. Do you know how many statements you made? One or more?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a full answer to that question. Please allow me to tell you how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I will not allow you. I'm just asking: One or more statements.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- I can't answer that question. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When you were before the military court in Belgrade, my colleague asked you in detail about the exchange. But before you were exchanged, did the court actually pass a decision whereby they were relieving you of all responsibility?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the -- what the sentence was, prescribed sentence for armed rebellion?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know today?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The next question: You answered today when my colleague asked you, put that question, you said that at the beginning of August some buildings were shelled, among them a building housing officers of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the building itself but the area in front or outside the building because this was right next to the hospital building.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the answer now?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my answer is, in August, in 1992, on August 13th --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What happened with the -- with the building housing JNA officers?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building housing JNA officers, a shell landed outside the building and this was almost in the hospital -- on the hospital perimeter, and I don't know exactly what happened. I think a car was demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, tell us, were officers only housed in that building or were there other people?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were also civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were these those officers who shelled the building from the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know who actually shelled this building from the barracks, but I know that's where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you think it is logical for officers from the barracks to fire at the building where their families and wives and children lived? What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, all I can say now is that it was possible because they had already removed their families and put them in barracks so there was no reason for them not to fire these.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: So would you then agree with the proposition that -- or would you agree, would you state that everyone who was firing from the barracks was at that time in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I don't know exactly where they were. I really couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, how could you tell us -- how can you claim, then, that they had all disappeared from the building, since politics was not something that you were interested in, you were really involved with the hospital and this -- how did you learn of this fact?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because my own flat is across the road from that building and my family lives across the road from that building, and the hospital is also across from there, and, of course, we could see if there were people inside or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To my friend's question, you said that the ZNG was under the command of the MUP of Vukovar. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that they were under the command of the Ministry of the Interior, and there was a Vukovar branch so that was where their command was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that Stipo Pole as the commander in Vukovar could give orders to the people who belonged to the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that he was also the superior of Ivica Arbanas? I'm sorry, I first have to ask you do you know who Ivica Arbanas is?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do, because he would come in the hospital bringing in wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What wounded?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The wounded -- wounded who were members of the ZNG. But also I think he brought on his back a member of the Serbian Chetnik formation known as Pavlo Teofanovic. That's his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was he the chief commander of the paramilitary known as the ZNG in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know who the commander was. Later on I know when Jastreb arrived, it was said that he had taken over the command pursuant to orders from Zagreb over the ZNG.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that point in time, was there a Vukovar Territorial Defence or not, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you aware that the Territorial Defence had previously consisted of both Croats and Serbs, before these events?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence, I don't know. It was within the competence, as far as I can recall, of the then Secretariat for National Defence in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, thank you. My next question: We said, after Mr. Domazet put a question to you, that when this was happening in Vukovar a member of the Supreme Command of the JNA was Stipe Mesic, who is a Croat, and under whose command, together with the other members of the collective organ of the JNA was. Do you agree with this again?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You have to ask Stipe Mesic what circumstances he was operating in and whether he was just a figure-head or not. I'm not competent to answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I think you have. I think you said a while ago that he was there formerly as president of the Presidency which was the Supreme Command of the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you before that he was in fact -- maybe the best expression is a figure-head, not formally but figuratively.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: That's sufficient. So the answer is the jury. The next question is: Did you take an oath when you served in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I also took the oath of Hippocrates.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: We will come back to that. But my question is: In the text of this oath, does it say that you undertake to, if necessary, protect with your life the territorial integrity of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: While it was that, while there was some kind of equality, yes. The moment that Yugoslavia dissolved, the moment that, as you know well, Yugoslavia disappeared as such, in my deep conviction that oath lost its meaning after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But was the text what I told you?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the text of the oath. You probably read it when preparing for this cross-examination. But it's been 30 and more years since I saw the text, so I don't remember what it said exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: But do you confirm that there was a solemn oath taken when entering the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The JNA of which the Supreme Commander at that point in time was Stipe Mesic, did it set out toward Vukovar to protect the territorial integrity of the country or do you treat it as a paramilitary formation? This is rather a broad question, but you say that you broke that oath when, in your view, the country ceased to exist. Is it your own view that matters or are there precise standards in the army?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took the JNA oath while I was a member of that army. I think that after that it was no longer binding upon me. As for Stipe Mesic and the command of the JNA, I'm not competent to answer that. You should ask him that. He knows what he was responsible for. I can be responsible only for my own actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Who was the secretary for National Defence during these events in Vukovar; do you know?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what time period you mean. Could you please be more precise in your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I'll be very precise. From the point when the secretary of National Defence, who was a Serb, was replaced, Mercep was appointed in his place. Do you know when that was?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know precisely when, but I think it was in June, maybe May. I'm not sure. I cannot tell you even an approximate date. I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you still a member of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: While you were a minister in the HDZ government, can you tell me what Serbs were ministers and for what at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but Pavlovic, Juzbasic. There were others later on. But if you were to ask me what the composition of the government was from 1992 onwards, it would be very hard for me to enumerate names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I meant ministers of Serb ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were you in favour of the secession of Croatia and the creation of an independent Croatian state which is part of the HDZ platform?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the HDZ platform from before. I can only speak of the platform of 1992, after it was quite clear what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were you in favour of that project regardless of the HDZ platform?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you about the HDZ platform that you want to impute to me. I'm telling you only what I know. I accepted that platform at a time when Croatia was already internationally recognised as an independent, sovereign and democratic state.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But while you were in the Vukovar Hospital, when you're testifying about the events in Vukovar Hospital, was Croatia internationally recognised then, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some countries had already recognised Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what international recognition means? You're an educated man. Was it formally internationally recognised at the time of the events in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you allow for the possibility that it wasn't?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I also allow for the possibility that it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. It will be easy to prove that it wasn't. Do you know, and have you heard of, the Guards Brigade? What does that title mean?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: By that I understand the ZNG. If the ZNG is a guards brigade, then that's what it is, but I'm no military expert, and I'm not familiar with military vocabulary. For that reason, I cannot give you a precise answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It's quite the opposite. A guards brigade is part of the regular JNA, while the ZNG, as we heard today, was part of the Ministry of the Interior of Croatia. It was therefore a paramilitary formation. I'm asking you about the guards brigade of the JNA. Did you hear about it during the events in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ZNG is not a paramilitary formation. It's a regular military formation, as you know well. You're trying to put words in my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard that it's a military -- a regular military formation?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular police formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute. As you said that it was a regular military formation, now when I say military, you say police. Is it military or police? Be precise.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm giving you the same answer I gave to Mr. Domazet when we were clarifying this. I said, in answer to his question, that that is a military -- that is the ZNG, the National Guard Corps, is part of the MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, which means that they are members of the police, and I assume it's a kind of special police unit, not military. Later on, it became part of the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At the point in time I'm asking you about now, we hear that there is the MUP, Ministry of the Interior, and as you say, the ZNG, which was part of the MUP. Did Croatia have its own military force or not?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia at the time had only members of the police and as part of the police forces the National Guard Corps. But excuse me, let me complete my thought. I am not competent to clarify what police forces consist of or how the police is organised or how military units are organised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But as you have given yourself the role of someone who is conversant with these issues and gave us an explanation of what the ZNG was, and I asked you whether Croatia had a military force at the time, you gave me this answer. Let's move on. Did you publish a book about these events?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What is the title?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Head Down, Hands Behind Your Back."

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me how many copies were issued?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask the publisher, nor have I ever been paid.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you described how the JNA came to the hospital for the first time. You described an officer who came for the first time as you said yesterday. Would you tell the Court how tall this officer was?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me what he looked like?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Does it mean you wouldn't be able to recognise him?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I would be able to recognise the face. It's the face we mostly remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you see -- recognise him easily because you saw his face in the Croatian media? Would that be why you could recognise his face?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. When we thought we would all be exchanged, and finally --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, I don't want to interrupt you often but we do want to focus. If we have long answers to issues I haven't asked about, this will take a very long time. I will be very precise in my question. Did you see in the media from 1991 onwards to today photographs of Mrksic, Radic and Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't need -- let me finish. Your Honours, please, when I am answering, may I be allowed to clarify? May I be allowed to say and respond in the way I feel I should? Briefly, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Of course I will not prevent the witness from explaining, but I think I do have the right, when the witness is trying to avoid giving a direct answer and is speaking at great length, I feel I have the right to interrupt him. What I'm asking you is in this past 15 years --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Doctor, the process in this courtroom is assisted if you listen to questions that are put to you and answer those questions. I have noticed it is quite often the case that you will deal with one, two or three other matters and then answer the question that is put to you. It would be of assistance if you were able to focus your answers more, specifically on the question. When you do answer the question, you certainly will be allowed to answer it as fully as you feel is relevant, and you will notice that I don't believe any counsel has in the end stopped you from doing that so far. So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, kindly, Your Honours. Thank you. This is my answer: I saw Mr. Sljivancanin and Mr. Radic, and I could see them hundred times more later on the television, and still never forget their faces. As for Mr. Mrksic, I saw him for the first time on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that the witness saw them in the last 15 years in the media?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Next question: Can the witness describe the uniform worn at the time by Captain Radic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Radic came in the uniform of a JNA captain. It was an olive drab-type uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What did he have on his head?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: On his head, I really can't recall, just like I can't recall what other people wore on their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about his ranks?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on his shoulder, on his epaulettes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you served in the army, how many stars were there?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see a weapon he had?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't pay attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said that he came in military vehicles. You described the barrels. My question is: This military vehicle, did it have a caterpillar-type wheels or regular wheels?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regular wheels.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about barrels?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Large barrels pointed at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Large calibre or small?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me too much. It was a larger calibre than what I had seen prior to that, say, on a machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. All right. Yesterday and today, you said that the JNA had taken away the documentation in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what barracks do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Not barracks, the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The hospital documentation was put in a sack by a soldier and taken away. Everything that I've mentioned. All register books, case histories and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you burn some documents upon the arrival of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you take any papers with you when you left for the investigative prison?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Had I taken it with me, it would have been taken away from me because in Mitrovica they strip-searched us and took everything away from us. They seized it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Everything that is stated in your book, is it true and do you stand by it?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by the portion written by me, but there are also parts written by other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If I were to tell you that I read your book and if it says in your book, and you can confirm this or I can put it to you, that you burned all of the documentation except for the decision appointing you head of the war staff, what would you say about that? Is it true or not?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are mixing up things. Confusing things, sir. I had an ID indicating that I was appointed a reserve member of the MUP and commander of medical services. I was appointed that by the main medical staff. Therefore, I kept only the portion appointing me commander of medical services during wartime. The other bit I gave to my wife who burned it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When were you able to give it to your wife to burn it if the JNA arrived?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Moore?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: The question that is posed is at 76, I think it's 18:44:25. "Thank you. If I were to tell you that I had read your book, I say it's your book and you confirm this, I put it to you that you burnt all of the documentation except the decision appointing you head of the war staff." Is my learned friend saying all of the documentation vis-a-vis the documentation that the doctor said was put in a sack or is he referring to documentation that relates to his personal identification? We have not heard any reference to it, and there has to be more precision in relation to the question itself. What documentation is he supposed to have burnt? No use my learned friend saying I've read it and this is the way it is. He's got to give the witness a chance to deal with the specifics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic, I think things moved on rapidly there, but Mr. Moore has brought us back to what was your opening question and it is an appropriate observation he makes, that the question you put at the beginning of this portion was very vague and needs to be clarified. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, not only you are right but also my learned friend, Mr. Moore. It is true we covered this quickly because I believe the witness to stand by his previous statements. But as I'm not putting anything from the book to him yet --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: Did you state in this book that you wanted to burn documentation - I'm not specifying which one - in order to prevent it from falling into the enemy's hands?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And I stand firmly behind this. I burnt my personal documentation, not official medical records. So personal documentation was burned except for this document which probably still exists in Mitrovica, document appointing me head of wartime medical services.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were assigned to the MUP of Croatia, you said that you had a wartime assignment in the MUP of Croatia. When was that?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody had to treat the wounded MUP members, so in order to show their gratitude for my treating the MUP members, they gave me an ID indicating - this was probably sometime in August or September --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who gave you this ID showing that you were a member of the MUP of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a member, but a member of reserve forces. If I remember well, I was given this by the then commander, Stipe Pole.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you be so kind as to tell us, as a reserve member of the MUP of Croatia, did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know what the abbreviation KOS means?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please tell the Court?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: When did you hear this for the first time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of us who served in the JNA knew about KOS, counter-intelligence service. Its task, at least I assume so, was to protect the state, the state elite, and institutions. Of course, this is not a precise definition. I don't know much about the work of this institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Have you ever met a member of KOS, counter-intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. While I served in the garrison clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Where?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Petrovaradin, which is a section of Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was that the last time you ever met a member of KOS?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe I did later, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean later? Recently? In recent years?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I simply don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have an official conversation with any member of KOS or not?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Sremska Mitrovica upon my capture.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of that member of KOS?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: He introduced himself as lieutenant colonel and said his name was Stanko.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you say perhaps that there was a man called Gojko with the same function?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a Gojko, I think a major, a specialist in pulmonology who told me that he was commander of war medical services in Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Did you, on that occasion, give a statement, an official statement, to the members of KOS or not?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I gave a statement at their request and upon being examined to Colonel Stanko.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. You're using these names freely. Gojko, Stanko. And you remembered last names of the people with whom you had dealings prior to that. So do you remember their last names?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But I think this can be easily verified in the records in Sremska Mitrovica. I'm sure that there weren't too many colonels with the first name Stanko.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who brought you to Sremska Mitrovica? Was it a member of KOS?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They sat in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All I'm asking is, was it a member of KOS?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Dr. Radomir Dejanovic is?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Radomir Dejanovic is a young colleague, who, upon completing his internship showed interest in surgery. I recommended him to my boss, said that he should be admitted -- or rather, employed and allowed to begin his surgical residency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know where he studied?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My next question pertains to the 18th of November, 1991, the date that you gave testimony about in the last two days. My first question is: Did you hear about Major Tesic?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: The second question: You stated that a captain had come out. Was he accompanied by a major?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any majors.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was there or wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't remember that there was a major present or accompanying captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us whether the captain introduced himself?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Not right then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who else accompanied him?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: A soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just one soldier?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right then, when we were expecting the representatives of the International Red Cross as well, we were naturally surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No. All I'm asking is whether there was somebody else apart from the soldier?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a soldier. Whether there were other people there as well, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Next question: How many soldiers provided security to the hospital, as you have already told us that they had to cover all openings, as you picturesquely described it to you. So since they had to cover all openings, please tell us roughly how many soldiers were assigned to the security of the hospital at the time when the JNA entered the hospital for the first time?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they entered the hospital, we went into the basement. After that, the soldiers came, and I can enumerate these openings, large ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, just tell us roughly.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: One, two, three, four, five, six, about a dozen openings. Larger and smaller ones. There was not a single window pane left intact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. But were there any other JNA soldiers providing external security for the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't see that because we were indoor, so we didn't know whether there were or weren't. We only saw the ones standing at the openings. Those that were visible.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. In addition to you, who else was there when the JNA arrived?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: In addition to me, Dr. Bosanac and Martin Vidic, Bili.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You mean Marin?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. Yes, I mean Marin Vidic, Bili.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that at that point in time they were elsewhere, what would be your comment?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But after that, they went away. Right then they were with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Well, how come, when all of you went into the basement --

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I went into the basement. I didn't say anything about the others, because, the others, as far as I know, probably started negotiating about vacating the hospital on the 19th.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but just several sentences ago, and we can see this in the transcript, you stated we went into the basement.

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. That was a slip of tongue. I went into the basement. I don't know what they did. All I know is that as far as I can remember on the 18th in the evening, they were not at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. How many people were there, then, in your estimate?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to pinpoint the exact number. There were a lot of wounded, more than 450, and there were also a lot of those who had arrived from the basements in town and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. All right. I'm not going to torture you any longer with this. Did you send faxes and did you make phone calls to Vinkovci and other national associations, organisations?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that Dr. Bosanac, while giving testimony here, on the 27th of October, in transcript on page 4, line 9, said she wasn't the only one who sent faxes and appeals, "many of us did that, Dr. Njavro and Marin Vidic," would that affect your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that at one point in time, I sent a fax. However, the documentation which is most likely together with other documentation one could check this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Can you please tell us who might you have sent this fax to?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I did send a fax, all of us sent it to the same address more or less, the international observers in the Hotel I in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said all of us. Does that mean Vesna Bosanac and who else?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I meant the inner circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Which would be who?

utterances.speaker: JURAJ NJAVRO [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vesna, Bili and I. Although there were other colleagues as well who were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Mr. Borovic? If you're chasing a particular point, we can go a minute or two but no longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will comply with your suggestion, Your Honour. Let us take a break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 15th day of November, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
